description:
🚀 #EraConTuto | NASA Space Apps Challenge

Somos un equipo con ideas fuera de este mundo y café suficiente para intentar hacerlas realidad.

Creamos una solución tecnológica para monitorear la salud de los astronautas durante sus misiones espaciales, combinando programación, creatividad y muchas horas sin dormir.

En la Tierra hacemos código. En el espacio, tratamos de no romper nada. 🌌
summary:
CUSTODIA is a free browser game where players aged 7 to 12 design and run a ten-day space mission. You are an astronaut on a Space Station, Moon or Mars base whose AI is failing, and the rescue ship is ten days away. To get home you must keep four connected systems alive (life support, power, radiation shielding and food), handle emergencies, and decide what to do when a solar storm arrives.

It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning real NASA data into decisions with a cost. Storms come from real solar flares in NASA’s DONKI database; sheltering saves radiation dose but costs time and power, while continuing adds a dose that never goes away.

It matters because NASA’s open science rarely reaches children in a form they can use. CUSTODIA lets a child learn it by playing, with no account, no installation, and no reading level required.
details:
What it does. CUSTODIA is a top-down survival and mission-management game that runs in any browser. The player picks a destination (Space Station, Moon or Mars) and a difficulty, then lives ten in-game days on a base. Each morning there is a maintenance shift for four systems: life support, power, radiation shielding and food. The systems are connected: low power makes the others degrade faster, and weak shielding raises the daily radiation dose. Three solar storms hit during each mission. When the warning sounds, the player chooses between running to the shelter (almost no dose, but the current task is lost and the shelter drains power) or continuing to work (the dose adds up and is never erased). After each storm a card compares the player’s dose with the shelter dose and with NASA’s real career limit. The mission is won when the rescue ship arrives with the crew alive.

Benefits. Children learn why astronauts follow routines and protocols by experiencing the trade-offs. A Cadet mode for ages 7–12 lowers damage and adds helpers; a seven-step guided tutorial, read-aloud, and a closing question support early readers. Teachers get a class mode with a results panel and CSV export, and winners receive a Cadet certificate. The game works offline after the first visit and can be installed on a computer, tablet or phone. It is available in Spanish and English with recorded AI voice lines, and in Hebrew as text.

Intended impact. To make NASA’s open data usable by primary-school children, including classrooms with weak connectivity, and to show that space science is a series of understandable decisions.

NASA data used. Solar flares from NASA DONKI (live, with an archived fallback that the game discloses); the NASA-STD-3001 career radiation limit of 600 mSv; measured daily doses for the ISS, the Moon (Chang’e-4) and Mars (Curiosity RAD); health findings cited from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository; and simplified ISS emergency procedures from NASA technical reports. Every protocol is labelled as real, real risk with game steps, or fiction, and game-scale numbers are identified as such.

Tools and languages. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules) with Canvas 2D and the Web Audio API, with no game engine and no external dependencies. Node.js runs the 236 automated logic tests, a balance simulator and a small local server. Cooperative play uses WebSocket and WebRTC. A service worker provides offline play. Git and GitHub for collaboration. AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) supported programming, analysis and documentation, and Higgsfield generated the AI character’s voice lines; the team made the design decisions.

How it is creative. The base’s own AI is the antagonist: it watches the crew and, on higher difficulties, learns the player’s routes and hiding places. A two-player mode pairs an Astronaut with a Mission Control player whose orders arrive with a signal delay on the Moon and Mars. The radiation lesson is taught through one repeated choice, never through a lecture.

What the team considered. Age-appropriate content with no graphic violence and a soft visual mode without shaking or flashes; honesty about what is real and what is simplified; accessibility for early readers and for phones; playability without an account or internet; and replay value through three destinations, different storms, random threats and a daily challenge.
dataRefs: NASA-STD-3001, Volume 1, and the OCHMO Radiation Protection technical brief. Source of the 600 mSv career radiation limit shown after each storm, and of the ALARA principle.

NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS). ISS emergency procedures, heavily simplified for the protocol mini-games: 20030053429 and 20120002562 (fire detection, suppression and crew response), 20250003954 (fire, toxic spills and rapid depressurization), 20220019247 (toxic atmosphere, including ammonia leaks)
